UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                 FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

         Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC               )      Docket No. ER26-550-001


                            REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF
                           DUKE ENERGY CAROLINAS, LLC

         Pursuant to Section 313(a) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 and Rule 713 of the

Rules and Regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

“Commission”),2 Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (“DEC”) hereby files this Request for

Rehearing of the Commission’s August 7, 2026 Order issued in the above-referenced

docket.3 Rehearing of an order on rehearing is appropriate “when the order on rehearing

modifies the result reached in the original order in a manner that gives rise to a wholly new

objection.”4 Such is the case here.

         In its January 16 Order, the Commission stated that “the Commission’s policy is to

deny waiver of the prior notice requirement for rate increases.”5 As explained in DEC’s

request for rehearing, this is inconsistent with the Commission’s practice and application

of Prior Notice, as evidenced by repeated examples of the Commission granting waiver



1
    16 U.S.C. § 825l.
2
    18 C.F.R. § 385.713.
3
 Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, Order Addressing Arguments Raised on Rehearing, 196
FERC ¶ 61,117 (Aug. 7, 2026) (“August 7 Order”).

5
  Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, Docket No. ER26-550-000 (Jan. 16, 2026) (delegated

 under the same circumstance (including to the Kings Mountain Network Integration

Transmission Service Agreement itself). This proceeding is not about a routine rate

increase or an individualized request to begin new service to a new customer. It concerns

an amended service agreement implementing service under a filed tariff of general

applicability (an “umbrella” tariff). In its August 7 Order, the Commission revised its

reasoning. Now the Commission states its “policy is to deny waiver of the 60-day prior

notice requirement for rate increases for existing services” even in cases of uncontested

service agreements to which both the customer and transmission provider mutually agree

on their terms and conditions.6 This new explanation, premised not on a blanket application

of Prior Notice to all agreements, but based on a distinction between new and existing

services, is novel and engenders different objections.      Accordingly, consistent with

Commission precedent, Duke seeks rehearing of the August 7 Order.7

         This new and narrowed interpretation of Prior Notice has no basis in Commission

policy or precedent. Rehearing is warranted because the August 7 Order creates a wholly

new rationale to justify the January 16 Order’s denial of DEC’s waiver, marking a

significant—and unjustified—change in Commission policy.          Under well-established

principles of administrative law, the Commission must recognize and justify the change

and explain its reasons. Because the August 7 Order did not, it should be set aside on

rehearing.



6
    August 7 Order at P 14 (emphasis added).
7
    ISO New England Inc., 174 FERC ¶ 61,120 at P 4.


                                               2
        Moreover, the change in policy creates significant and unnecessary burdens for the

customers and transmission providers that the Commission does not address. Under this

new policy, transmission providers can no longer utilize a 30-day post commencement time

period in which to finalize, tender, and execute routine service agreement revisions and

must delay providing the requested service for 61 days into the future to abide by the new

Commission policy allowing requested effective dates to be no earlier than 61 days in the

future. This is the case even for service agreements that are uncontested and received the

mutual agreement of both the customer and transmission provider as to their terms and

conditions. Additionally, transmission providers are now exposed to increased risk of

penalties for non-compliance with the new policy (including payment of time value

refunds) if service commences prior to 61 days after agreement execution. Finally,

customers are disadvantaged by this new policy because transmission providers can no

longer accommodate urgent or fast-moving electric service transactions under service

agreements without now waiting 61 days for the agreement to become effective prior to

providing such service. In many instances, fast-moving transactions are used to provide

revised network service to allow customers to serve new loads or to provide faster

interconnection service through engineering and procurement agreements, provisional

large generator interconnection agreements, or surplus large generator interconnection

agreements. These burdens warrant careful consideration of this change in policy.

I.     STATEMENT OF ISSUES AND SPECIFICATIONS OF ERROR

       Pursuant to Rule 713(c), DEC submits the following combined statement of issues

and specification of error:


                                            3
           1.    The Order is arbitrary and capricious, in violation of the Administrative
                Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, and otherwise contrary to law because it fails
                to provide a reasoned basis for departing from Commission precedent to deny
                DEC’s request for waiver of the requirement that rates and charges for
                jurisdictional service be filed at least 60 days before the commencement of
                such service.

II.       BACKGROUND

          On November 19, 2025, DEC submitted a NITSA between itself and the City of

Kings Mountain, North Carolina, to be filed under Tariff Volume No. 4 of DEC’s Joint

OATT, an umbrella tariff of general applicability.8 DEC requested an effective date of

November 1, 2025, consistent with the Commission’s longstanding policy of granting

waiver of the 60-day prior notice requirement for service agreements filed under an

umbrella tariff within 30 days after service commences.9 And, as Duke explained, the

Commission had granted similar waivers for amendments of the Kings Mountain NITSA

on several occasions.10 On January 16, 2026, the Commission issued a delegated letter

order denying waiver and instead accepting the Kings Mountain NITSA with an effective

date of January 19, 2026—61 days after filing.11 The January 16 Order did not address

DEC’s arguments concerning 18 C.F.R. § 35.3(a)(2) or the Commission’s longstanding

 Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, Revised Network Integration Transmission Service
Agreement with City of Kings Mountain, North Carolina, Docket No. ER26-550-000 (filed
Nov. 19, 2025) (“DEC November 19, 2025 Filing”).

11
     January 16 Order at 1.


                                              4
 waiver policy.12 It stated only that “the Commission’s policy is to deny waiver of the prior

notice requirement for rate increases.”13

         DEC filed a timely request for rehearing, which was deemed denied by operation of

law, and petitioned for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, pursuant

to 16 U.S.C. § 825l and Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC.14 On August 7, 2026, almost

nine months after DEC submitted the Kings Mountain NITSA, the Commission issued the

instant Order, in which it considered for the first time—and rejected—DEC’s arguments

that it was entitled to a waiver under the Commission’s policy announced in Prior Notice.

The August 7 Order added a novel, previously unannounced narrowing justification for the

denial: “the Commission’s policy is to deny waiver of the 60-day prior notice requirement

for rate increases for existing services.”15

required to be filed and posted authorizing a customer to take electric service under the
terms of a tariff, or any part thereof, shall be tendered for filing with the Commission and

may be specified by the Commission.”).

 III.     THE ORDER UNLAWFULLY DEPARTS FROM ESTABLISHED
         COMMISSION POLICY WITHOUT ADEQUATE EXPLANATION OR
         JUSTIFICATION

         A.     The Commission’s Policy Is To Grant Waiver For Service Agreements
                Filed Under Umbrella Tariffs Within 30 Days Of Service For All Services

         For over 30 years, it has been the Commission’s policy that, for service agreements

filed under umbrella tariffs, “waiver of notice will be granted if service agreements are

filed within 30 days after service commences.”16          The Commission routinely and

consistently applied this policy to grant waiver of notice for amended service agreements,

including agreements containing rate increases and including previous amendments to this

very agreement.17 DEC and other industry participants rely on the stability of this policy

to plan their business operations.18

     Prior Notice, 64 FERC ¶ at 61,984.

(Nov. 20, 2024) (accepting DEF-FMPA NITSA filed on September 26, 2024 effective as

2022 containing increase in distribution rates applicable to Point of Delivery Charges);
Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, Delegated Letter Order, Docket No. ER21-2223, at 1 & n.2

        A significant operational benefit of the flexibility of the ability to file service

agreements within 30 days after service has commenced is that it allows a transmission

provider to commence urgent or fast-moving electric service transactions immediately,

thereby avoiding the potentially costly and disruptive effect of waiting for a requested

effective date 61 days into the future. These operational benefits manifest in a variety of

ways such as: enabling urgent electric service transactions (including through revisions to

existing NITSAs) to serve new load, including new large loads, with in-service dates that

require prompt commencement of construction of network upgrades and/or direct

assignment facilities; enabling the execution of engineering and procurement agreements

under which customers seek to authorize the transmission provider to commence

procurement of long lead time materials to accommodate timely generator interconnection;

and allowing for provisional and surplus large generator interconnection agreements to

NCMPA1 NITSA filed on June 30, 2021 effective as of June 1, 2021 containing “a minor

and maintenance charge for the Blue Ridge Delivery No. 29 delivery point”); Duke Energy
Fla., LLC, Delegated Letter Order, Docket No. ER19-2391, at 1 (Aug. 20, 2019) (accepting
DEF-FMPA NITSA filed on July 12, 2019 effective as of July 1, 2019 containing increase

18
  See supra note 17; see also Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 191 FERC ¶ 61,102 (2025); Sw. Power
Pool, Inc., 171 FERC ¶ 61,086 (2020); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 154 FERC ¶ 61,280 (2016);
ISO New Eng. Inc., 178 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2022).


                                             7
 permit customers to take advantage of faster generator interconnections on an expedited

and/or short-term basis.

         Contrary to precedent and practice, the August 7 Order now claims that its policy

“does not apply to amendments to or revisions of service agreements to increase rates for

an existing service.”19 This distinction between new service and existing service appears

nowhere in the January 16 Order or the orders establishing the waiver policy, and is not

otherwise supported by the Commission’s precedent.

         In Central Hudson, the Commission stated that “absent a strong showing of good

cause, we will deny requests for waiver of notice for rate increases that do not implement

a contract requirement.”20 The Commission imposed an additional burden on agreements

for new service commenced before filing, holding that a utility must show “extraordinary

circumstances” to receive waiver in those circumstances.21 But the relevant distinction was

not between agreements for new service or existing service, but (1) filings that “do not

change rates” or “reduce rates,” for which waiver is “generally” granted; and (2) filings for

“rate increases that do not implement a contract requirement,” for which waiver is typically

denied absent good cause.22 This distinction enabled the Commission to “balance the

requirement that utilities promptly file their rates as embodied in the Federal Power Act




19
     August 7 Order at P 12.
20
     Cent. Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp., 60 FERC ¶ 61,106, 61,339 (1992).
21
     Id. at 61,339.
22
     Id. at 61,338–39.


                                             8
 and the need of utilities to transact business on short notice.”23 Whether a service is new

or existing was not dispositive. Central Hudson’s core inquiry was whether a filing

increased rates not implementing a contract requirement, not whether it was for new or

existing service.

           A year later, in Prior Notice, the Commission eliminated Central Hudson’s

extraordinary-circumstances requirement for the filing of service agreements under

umbrella tariffs. In practice, it found Central Hudson overly “restrictive” and “stifling” of

short-term deals, particularly where the service was being provided under an umbrella

tariff.24 The Commission recognized that umbrella tariffs enabled the efficient completion

of “short-term, economic transactions that . . . benefit all parties to the transactions.”25

Accordingly, to “encourage the use of umbrella tariffs which allow substantial transactional

flexibility,” Prior Notice “relax[ed]” Central Hudson’s onerous test and instead determined

that, for service agreements filed under umbrella tariffs, “waiver of notice will be granted

if service agreements are filed within 30 days after service commences.”26

           In the years since Prior Notice, these considerations have become stronger due to

changing business and market conditions, including the higher volume of service

agreements being entered into. DEC has reported 248 transmission service agreements on

its second quarter 2026 Electric Quarterly Report (“EQR”) filing, and its affiliates Duke

     Id. at 61,339.

 Energy Florida, LLC and Duke Energy Progress, LLC have reported 178 and 172 service

agreements respectively on their corollary EQRs. The Duke southeast utilities therefore

have 598 service agreements on file. The Commission’s unannounced change to its policy

concerning service agreements entered into under umbrella tariffs materially complicates

the administration of these agreements and “stifles” their usefulness.

       Further, there is a present-day need to accommodate more prompt generator

interconnections in a time of significant generation build-out through service agreements

such as engineering and procurement agreements, provisional large generator

interconnection service agreements, and surplus interconnection service agreements to

serve load growth. And, there is also a need to timely commence construction activities to

accommodate changes in network integration transmission service under NITSAs to

provide customers with network service to serve growing and new loads (including large

loads) in an age of unprecedented load growth in the Carolinas region.27


27
   The Duke Energy 2025 Annual Report highlighted increasing load growth in the
Carolinas, stating that “[o]ur territories continue to attract new business, with North
Carolina named the Top State for Business by CNBC for the third time in four years and
Florida, North Carolina and South Carolina ranking among the top five states for
population growth.” Duke Energy, 2025 Annual Report and Form 10-K at 2, https://annual-
report.duke-energy.com. The 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan filed by DEC with the North
Carolina Utilities Commission reflects “increasing electricity demand across the Carolinas
at an unprecedented pace.” 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan, Executive Summary at 6,
https://www.duke-energy.com/our-company/about-us/irp-carolinas/2025-crp. The plan
states that customer energy needs over the past 15 years increased by approximately 10
terawatt-hours and is forecasted to grow to 8 times that amount in the next 15 years. Id.
In 2025 alone, the North Carolina Department of Commerce highlighted that “companies
have announced economic development projects, producing more than 25,000 jobs and
$19 billion in investments, the bulk of which is for new manufacturing facilities.” Id. The
South Carolina Department of Commerce recently announced “5,500 new jobs and $8.19
billion in capital investment in 2024.” Id. at 6–7.


                                            10
          The August 7 Order claims that “Prior Notice does not apply to amendments to or

revisions of service agreements to increase rates for an existing service.”28 But Prior

Notice contains no such limitation, and there is no basis in precedent for it. As Prior Notice

made clear, the scope of waiver turns on whether the service is covered by an umbrella

tariff, not whether the filing is for new or existing service. The August 7 Order identifies

no basis in the text of 18 C.F.R. § 35.3 to exclude existing service. Rather, it derives the

limitation from a newly elevated interpretation of Prior Notice and Central Hudson. As

DEC has explained, the January 16 Order erroneously applied Section 35.3(a)(1) to the

Kings Mountain NITSA to deny waiver.29 Section 35.3(a)(2) applies to customer-specific

service agreements under an umbrella tariff.30          Section 35.3(a)(1) establishes the

Commission’s general filing rule for rate schedules, tariffs, and service agreements.

Section 35.3(a)(2), by contrast, specifically addresses service agreements under umbrella

tariffs and establishes a distinct filing regime for those agreements. FERC does not dispute

that the revised Kings Mountain NITSA was (1) filed under an umbrella tariff and (2) is a

customer-specific service agreement. Because the Kings Mountain NITSA is concededly

a service agreement under an umbrella tariff, section 35.3(a)(2) governs unless the

regulation expressly excludes the filing from that subsection.

         The August 7 Order claims the date that service commences for all service

agreements under section 35.3(a)(2) is based on the date of the original agreement and thus


28
     August 7 Order at P 12.
29
     DEC February 13 Request for Rehearing at 5–6.
30
     18 C.F.R. § 35.3(a)(2).


                                             11
 the section cannot apply to existing service.31 But there is nothing in text or precedent to

support that claim. Central Hudson stated that, for “filings that provide for new service

that is not pursuant to an accepted contract or settlement,” the Commission “will continue

to determine whether an agreement is filed prior to the commencement of service based on

the original filing date.”32 It did not extend this to existing service like the Kings Mountain

NITSA. And yet the August 7 Order does just that in an effort to limit section 35.3(a)(2)

to new service. There is nothing in the text of section 35.3(a)(2) or the Commission’s

precedent to support that limitation.

         If the Commission wishes to narrow Prior Notice beyond the regulatory text and

precedent to exclude agreements for existing service, it must recognize that it is doing so

and explain why. An agency cannot “depart from a prior policy sub silentio.”33

         B.     The Order Is An Unlawful Change In Commission Policy Without
                Adequate Justification or Explanation

         An agency’s unexplained departure from its own settled precedent is the paradigm

of arbitrary and capricious action that violates the APA. It is “textbook administrative law”

that the Commission must “provide a reasoned explanation for departing from precedent

or treating similar situations differently.”34 At minimum, the Commission must “display

awareness that it is changing position.”35 It must “indicat[e] that prior policies and


31
     August 7 Order at P 16.
32
     Central Hudson, 60 FERC ¶ at 61,339.
33
     FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009).
34
     W. Deptford Energy, LLC v. FERC, 766 F.3d 10, 20 (D.C. Cir. 2014).

 standards are being deliberately changed, not casually ignored.”36 If “an agency glosses

over or swerves from prior precedents without discussion,” it crosses the line “from the

tolerably terse to the intolerably mute.”37 Accordingly, this change-in-position doctrine

asks (1) whether an agency changed its existing policy and (2) whether the agency

“‘display[ed] awareness that it is changing position’ and offer[ed] ‘good reasons for the

new policy.’”38

           The August 7 Order flunks this test. First, the Order marks an unmistakable change

in Commission policy. An agency changes its policy when it “acts inconsistently with an

earlier position, performs a reversal of its former views as to the proper course, or disavows

prior inconsistent agency action as no longer good law.”39 By its own terms, the Order

“acknowledge[s] that the Commission’s precedent is not entirely consistent” and disavows

all “Commission orders that have granted waiver of prior notice where a service agreement

included a rate increase for an existing service.”40 Under Supreme Court precedent, that is

enough to show a change in policy.41

           Second, the Commission provides no explanation for this shift in policy. The

January 16 Order stated that “the Commission’s policy is to deny waiver of the prior notice

                                               13
 requirement for rate increases.”42 As DEC explained in its Request for Rehearing, this was

inconsistent with prior Commission policy as the Commission previously had made no

distinction for service agreements. Rather than addressing DEC’s arguments, the August

7 Order now says something different: “the Commission’s policy is to deny waiver of the

60-day prior notice requirement for rate increases for existing services.”43 The addition of

“for existing services” denotes a material policy change with no basis in Prior Notice or

the Commission’s other precedent.

         This is not a one-off anomaly. On August 10, 2026, mere days after the August 7

Order, the Commission issued an order nearly identical to the August 7 Order here, stating

“the Commission’s policy is to deny waiver of the 60-day prior notice requirement for rate

increases for existing services.”44 The same rhetorical shift days apart in multiple dockets

shows that the Commission is undertaking a policy change sub silentio.

         That silence is unlawful. The Commission must “display awareness” of the change

and offer “good reasons” for it.45 The August 7 Order does neither. To the contrary, the

August 7 Order suggests that the Commission’s new policy is not new at all and simply an

application of New England Power Company—a 1995 order in which the Commission

granted waiver of the prior notice requirement.46 The August 7 Order points to a footnote

 stating that the New England Power Company (NEPCO) erroneously categorized its filing

as a filing for new service. From that dictum, the August 7 Order concludes that New

England explained that Prior Notice does not apply to amendments or revisions. But New

England is no beacon of Commission policy. The August 7 Order is the first time that DEC

is aware that the Commission ever cited New England for establishing this proposition. In

sharp contrast, the Commission has routinely granted waivers of the prior notice

requirements for amendments to service agreements since the issuing of New England and

without ever mentioning New England.47 Either way, then, the August 7 Order “acts

inconsistently with an earlier position, performs a reversal of its former views as to the

proper course, or disavows prior inconsistent agency action as no longer good law.”48 That

is a change in policy that requires justification.

          In addition, the Commission must “be cognizant that longstanding policies may

have engendered serious reliance interests that must be taken into account.”49 A “summary

discussion” of a departure is not sufficient where there has been “decades of industry

reliance” on a prior policy.50 DEC relied on decades of Commission precedent to determine

when to file the Kings Mountain NITSA. Under Prior Notice and as the Commission

reaffirmed several times with respect to amendments to DEC’s own agreements,51 service

 agreements filed under umbrella tariffs could be filed within 30 days after service

commences. By the time the Commission announced its newfound interpretation that

amendments increasing rates for existing service were excluded from this policy, the period

during which DEC supposedly should have provided that notice had already passed.

       This unannounced departure from and modification of prior policy has adverse

impacts on customers and transmission providers. As explained above, customers that have

agreed to rate increases in revised service agreements will not be provided with the

requested service for at least 61 days under this new policy, as compared with previous

situations in which the customers could have been provided with such service immediately

upon execution of the revised service agreement which could have been filed with the

Commission up to 30 days later.        Additionally, customers seeking faster generator

interconnection service or revised network transmission service to serve new and growing

loads will be harmed because transmission providers will need to delay providing such

services for at least 61 days to permit an effective date of the service agreements to become

regulatorily enforceable under this new policy. Transmission providers will be unable to

utilize the 30-day buffer under the relevant regulation to accommodate the faster pace of

electric service in the modern era of significant generation build-out and growing loads and

must instead absorb regulatory lag into their business models for services to be provided

under transmission service agreements. These negative impacts that have the effect of

delaying service to customers will be multiplied by the number of service agreements

entered into, which for the Duke southeast utilities is approximately 600, and for other even

larger transmission providers will be in the thousands.


                                             16
        In sum, all of the negative impacts described above are consequences of the

Commission’s refusal to apply its settled policy to the Kings Mountain NITSA, and to deny

and delay customer-requested service changes under a service agreement with mutually

agreed upon rates. The negative effects of the Commission’s departure from its policy will

ripple through thousands of service agreements across the electric industry.

IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, DEC respectfully requests that the Commission grant

rehearing and accept the Kings Mountain NITSA effective as of November 1, 2025.
